screens.title: Introduction to Fabric SDKs and Client Application Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: You are about to learn why Fabric SDKs are the practical bridge between application code and a running Fabric network. An SDK handles low-level details like cryptographic signing, connection lifecycle, and endorsement orchestration so your team can focus on business logic. This matters because without the SDK you would be building protobuf messages, managing TLS, and coordinating endorsement flows by hand — tasks that are error-prone and costly in production. As you progress, you will learn the core client components the SDK manages: Wallets for storing identities, Gateways for orchestrating proposals and submissions, Network objects that represent channels, and Contract objects that map to deployed chaincode functions. You will also trace the two primary interaction patterns: submit transactions that change ledger state and evaluate transactions that read state. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these pieces fit together and what to watch out for when designing client-side logic, such as not reusing a single identity for many users and never trying to replace the SDK with raw network calls. Consider how your current application would change if the SDK handled signing and peer orchestration for you.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build a clear mental model of the client-side pieces that make Fabric usable from application code. First, you will be able to explain why Fabric SDKs are necessary: they remove protocol and cryptography complexity so applications remain secure and maintainable. Second, you will identify and describe the four primary components a client application uses — Wallets, Gateways, Networks, and Contracts — and know how the SDK represents each. Third, you will trace the end-to-end interaction flow for both submitting a ledger-changing transaction and evaluating a read-only query, so you can reason about performance and security implications. Finally, you will be able to distinguish the responsibilities of Fabric network components — peers, orderers, and certificate authorities — from a client perspective and make design choices like where to route queries. Each objective includes a small skill you can verify in code or architecture diagrams, and the milestone indicates readiness to implement a basic Node. js client that connects, signs, and invokes chaincode. These skills matter because they keep your application correct, auditable, and resilient as it interacts with a permissioned ledger.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen translates the chapter goals into concrete skills you can demonstrate. You will load an identity from a Wallet and use it to authenticate with a Gateway. That means you must understand certificate and private key handling so transactions are correctly signed. You will also select a Network object representing a channel and obtain a Contract to invoke chaincode functions. Practically, this translates into writing code that performs a connection using a connection profile, selects a channel, and calls submitTransaction or evaluateTransaction. A verified milestone is when your Node. js client can submit a simple ledger update and receive confirmation that the transaction was ordered and committed. Finally, you will practice secure identity handling: create distinct identities per user, keep private keys protected, and avoid sharing a single certificate across multiple end users. These milestones ensure your client implementation is auditable and aligned with Fabric's permissioned model. Ask yourself: can you trace a request from a user action through the Wallet, Gateway, endorsing peers, orderer, and back to committed state?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Milestones

Verified competency milestones

Small, verifiable tasks that show you can connect and interact with Fabric safely.

Load and use a Wallet identity
Load a certificate and private key, sign a transaction proposal, and authenticate with a Gateway.
Connect to a Network and Contract
Select a channel and obtain a Contract object to call chaincode methods.
Submit and confirm a transaction
Perform a submitTransaction and confirm ordering and commit to the ledger.

Safety checks

  • Use distinct identities per user to preserve auditability and least privilege.
  • Never store private keys in insecure locations; the Wallet should protect them.
  • Avoid bypassing the SDK; direct peer calls require extensive cryptographic and protocol handling.
When these checks pass, you are ready to implement a basic production-ready client prototype.

screens.title: Why Fabric SDKs exist
screens.narratorSegment: A Fabric SDK is a language-specific library that gives you a high-level, idiomatic A P I to interact with a Fabric network. In practice the SDK hides details like constructing protobuf messages, managing TLS connections, signing proposals with a private key, and orchestrating endorsement requests across multiple peers. The concrete effect is that your application can call friendly methods to load identities, connect to a gateway, and invoke contract functions without handling low-level network or crypto plumbing. An example: instead of serializing a transaction proposal and sending manual gRPC calls, you call a method like submitTransaction and the SDK coordinates proposing to endorsing peers, collecting endorsements, and forwarding the transaction to the ordering service. A common misconception is that using the SDK removes all responsibility for security; it does not. You still must manage identities securely and choose appropriate endorsement policies. Another misconception is that SDKs are optional because protocols are open — while you could manually implement the protocol, doing so introduces significant risk and maintenance burden. Key takeaway: use the SDK to reduce complexity and lower the chance of cryptographic or protocol errors while keeping control of identity and policy decisions.

keyIdea.title: SDK simplifies complexity
keyIdea.text: Use SDKs to avoid low-level protocol and crypto work while maintaining secure identity management and policy choices.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why Fabric SDKs exist

Definition and role

An SDK provides high-level APIs that abstract gRPC, TLS, and signing, letting developers focus on business logic.

Concrete example
Calling submitTransaction instead of manually serializing and sending protobufs.
Common misconception
SDK use does not absolve you from secure identity handling or policy design.
Why it matters
Reduces errors and accelerates development, lowering risk in production deployments.
Key Takeaway

SDKs are essential productivity and safety tools; they do the heavy lifting while leaving security decisions to you.

The central teaching visual below shows the mental model: app code calls SDK methods; the SDK handles signing, endpoint connections, and endorsement orchestration.
Developer call
// Pseudocode style illustration
const wallet = await Wallets.newFileSystemWallet('./wallet')
const gateway = new Gateway()
await gateway.connect(connectionProfile, { wallet, identity: 'Alice' })
const network = gateway.getNetwork('mychannel')
const contract = network.getContract('assetContract')
await contract.submitTransaction('CreateAsset', 'asset1', 'blue', '5')
This snippet shows the high-level calls the SDK exposes; it hides signing and peer coordination details.
Notes
  • SDKs are available in Node.js, Java, Go, and Python.
  • They wrap lower-level client libraries and utilities.
  • Adopt the SDK for maintainability and security.

screens.title: SDK Language Options and Node.js focus
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Fabric provides SDKs for multiple languages so teams can choose a familiar runtime. The chapter lists Node. js, Java, Go, and Python as supported environments. Node. js is often emphasized for web and enterprise applications because it fits well with server-side JavaScript stacks and has a broad ecosystem for web integration. Remember that language choice affects tooling, deployment patterns, and available helper libraries. A common example: when you build a web service that calls chaincode from Express or Fastify, using the Node. js SDK keeps your stack unified and reduces impedance between web routing and blockchain logic. A misconception to check is thinking the SDK enforces business logic; it does not — it only provides APIs to interact with the network. Another pitfall is assuming feature parity across language SDKs. While core capabilities like Gateway, Wallets, Networks, and Contracts are present, the maturity of helper utilities can differ. Key takeaway: choose the SDK that integrates best with your application stack and team skills, and validate the SDK's features before committing to it in production. SDK Language Options and Node.js focus means choose the language sdk that aligns with your stack and team — node.js is common for web apps but verify feature parity.. In practical terms, node.js, java, go, and python — why node.js is a common choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Language SDKs
Node.js
Common for web and enterprise apps; integrates with JavaScript stacks and web frameworks.
Java
Useful for JVM ecosystems and enterprise integration with existing Java services.
Go
Lightweight and performant; often used where binaries and microservices are Go-based.
Python
Good for scripting, automation, and teams already using Python in data workflows.

Why focus on Node.js?

The chapter focuses on Node.js due to its popularity for web applications and a comprehensive feature set in the Fabric ecosystem. It often simplifies integration with REST APIs and front-end services.

Concrete scenario
A web service written in Node uses the Node.js SDK to sign and submit transactions on behalf of authenticated users, keeping the same language across the stack.
Misconception
Don't assume Node.js SDK features are identical to others; check available utilities and maturity for your use case.
Evaluate your team's skills and integration needs before selecting the SDK for production work.

screens.title: Wallets: secure identity stores
screens.narratorSegment: A Wallet in Fabric is a secure store for cryptographic credentials: typically a user's public certificate and corresponding private key. The SDK uses the wallet to retrieve an identity when signing transaction proposals or authenticating with a Gateway. The Wallet can be file-system-backed, in-memory, or implemented with external secret managers depending on your security needs. A concrete example: you might store separate identities for Alice and Bob in a FileSystem wallet during development, but in production you would use a hardware security module or a vault to protect private keys. A common mistake is using a single shared identity for all application users; this destroys auditability and violates the permissioned model. Another pitfall is leaving private keys unprotected on disk. The essential design choice is to map application users to distinct identities and protect the private keys with the appropriate storage mechanism. Key takeaway: treat the Wallet as the critical boundary for identity protection — design secure storage and not a convenience list of keys. Wallets: secure identity stores means store each user identity separately and protect private keys; wallets are the security boundary for signing and auditability.. In practical terms, what a wallet holds and why identity separation matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Wallet

What a Wallet contains

Public certificate, private key, and identity metadata used by the SDK to sign and authenticate.

Example
Use a FileSystem wallet for development and a secure vault or HSM for production to protect private keys.
Common mistake
Sharing one identity across many users breaks audit trails and increases risk.
Key Takeaway

Design your wallet strategy early: per-user identities, secure storage, and clear lifecycle policies.

Wallet types
FileSystem, in-memory, HSM or external key vault integrations depending on environment and threat model.
Mapping users to identities
Assign each application user a distinct identity for secure signing and auditability.

screens.title: Gateway: the orchestration point
screens.narratorSegment: The Gateway is the SDK component that sits between your application and the Fabric network, simplifying multi-peer interactions. When you submit a transaction, the Gateway accepts the request and orchestrates the proposal phase: it sends the proposal to the appropriate endorsing peers, collects endorsements, and sends the endorsed transaction to the ordering service. This centralization reduces the complexity your application needs to handle — you don't need to manage connections to every peer or collect endorsements manually. For queries, the Gateway typically forwards the evaluate call to a single peer for read-only execution, avoiding the ordering step. A concrete example: your app calls gateway. getNetwork('mychannel'). getContract('assetContract'). submitTransaction('UpdateAsset', 'asset1', 'red') and the Gateway does the heavy lifting. A common misconception is that the Gateway is a network component like a peer or orderer; it is not. It is an SDK abstraction or service that orchestrates client-facing steps. Key takeaway: the Gateway reduces client complexity and centralizes orchestration, but you should still design for redundancy and error handling at the application level. Gateway: the orchestration point means the gateway handles proposal distribution, endorsement collection, and submission to the orderer so the client remains simple.. In practical terms, how the gateway simplifies endorsement and submission for client apps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Gateway

Gateway responsibilities

  • Accepts signed proposals from the client.
  • For submit flows: sends proposals to endorsing peers and collects endorsements.
  • Submits endorsed transactions to the ordering service.
  • For evaluate flows: forwards query to a peer and returns the result.
Misconception
The Gateway is not a Fabric peer or orderer; it is the SDK-level orchestrator your application uses.
Concrete call sequence
gateway.connect(...); network = gateway.getNetwork('channel'); contract = network.getContract('cc'); contract.submitTransaction(...)
Key Takeaway

Rely on the Gateway to orchestrate multi-peer endorsement and ordering. Build resilient error handling around it.

screens.title: Network (Channel) and its role
screens.narratorSegment: In Fabric, a channel is an isolated ledger and policy boundary that hosts chaincode deployments. The SDK exposes a Network object that represents the channel you intend to interact with; it scopes all subsequent contract calls and peer interactions. When your application selects a network, you choose the channel whose ledger and chaincode instances you want to query or update. This separation allows multiple ledgers to coexist on the same physical network while keeping data isolated by policy. A practical example: a supply-chain deployment might use separate channels for different consortia; the client chooses the appropriate network when connecting so it only accesses the permitted ledger. A common misconception is treating a network object as a network transport; instead, it is a logical channel context within which contracts operate. Key takeaway: always select the correct Network to ensure you interact with the intended ledger and chaincode deployments, and remember channel-level policies control visibility and endorsement rules. Network (Channel) and its role means the network object scopes ledger access and contract interactions to a specific channel and its policies.. In practical terms, a network object represents a channel and provides access to deployed chaincode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Network (Channel)

Channel context and isolation

A Network object represents a specific channel and provides access to chaincode and peers on that channel.

Concrete scenario
Your app connects to 'supplychain-channel' to interact with assets visible only to that channel's members.
Misconception
A Network object is not a transport channel; it is the SDK view of a channel's ledger and deployed contracts.
Pick the network that maps to the ledger you must access. Channel-level endorsement policies and membership determine which peers will endorse and see the data.
Ledger scope
Each channel has its own ledger and world state.
Policy scope
Endorsement and access policies apply per channel.
Key Takeaway

Always interact with the correct Network object to respect ledger isolation and channel policies.

screens.title: Contracts (Chaincode) via the SDK
screens.narratorSegment: A Contract object in the SDK represents an instance of deployed chaincode on a channel and exposes the chaincode's functions as callable methods. The SDK allows you to call evaluateTransaction for read-only queries that do not change ledger state, or submitTransaction when you want to propose and commit a state change. Contracts are tied to the Network you selected, so the same chaincode name on different channels may refer to different deployments. A concrete example: if 'assetContract' implements CreateAsset and ReadAsset, your application calls contract. submitTransaction('CreateAsset', 'asset1', 'blue', '5') to create an asset and contract. evaluateTransaction('ReadAsset', 'asset1') to fetch its state. A common misconception is that calling a Contract method automatically commits state; only submitTransaction goes through endorsement and ordering to commit. Key takeaway: use Contract objects to encapsulate chaincode calls, choose submit or evaluate intentionally, and be mindful that contract behavior depends on the deployment and endorsement policies on the chosen channel. Contracts (Chaincode) via the SDK means use contract objects to call chaincode functions; pick submittransaction for writes and evaluatetransaction for reads.. In practical terms, how contract objects map to deployed chaincode functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Contract objects to call chaincode functions; pick submitTransaction for writes and evaluateTransaction for reads.

content.html:
Definition › Contract (Chaincode)

What a Contract provides

A callable interface to deployed chaincode functions within the selected channel context.

Example calls
contract.submitTransaction('CreateAsset', ...); contract.evaluateTransaction('ReadAsset', ...)
Remember: submitTransaction triggers endorsements and ordering; evaluateTransaction runs a read-only execution on a peer.
Deployment note
The Contract refers to the chaincode package deployed on the channel. Same names on different channels may differ.
Key Takeaway

Treat Contracts as the API surface to chaincode; choose methods that match read or write intent.

screens.title: End-to-end interaction flow
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing an end-to-end submit flow helps you reason about latency, reliability, and security. The typical sequence begins with loading an identity from the Wallet. That identity authenticates and signs proposals. Next, the application connects to a Gateway using the loaded identity and a connection profile that describes the network endpoints. The application then selects a Network (channel) and obtains a Contract. When the app calls submitTransaction, the Gateway creates a proposal and sends it to endorsing peers selected by policy. Each endorsing peer simulates the transaction and returns an endorsement. The Gateway collects endorsements and assembles an endorsed transaction, which it submits to the ordering service. The orderer packages transactions into blocks and distributes them to peers on the channel. Peers validate the transactions against endorsement policies and commit the block to their ledgers. Finally, the application can observe commit events or query the ledger to confirm the update. A common misconception is that submit returns final commit; often it returns after ordering and you should handle commit notifications or check ledger state. Key takeaway: understand each stage so you can instrument, retry, and secure your client properly.

keyIdea.title: Submit flow stages
keyIdea.text: Wallet -> Gateway -> Network -> Contract -> Endorsing peers -> Orderer -> Commit; instrument each stage for reliability.

content.html:
Process Flow › Submit transaction

Steps

  1. Load identity from Wallet and sign the request.
  2. Connect to Gateway with connection profile and identity.
  3. Select Network (channel) and get Contract.
  4. Call submitTransaction on the Contract.
  5. Gateway sends proposal to endorsing peers; collects endorsements.
  6. Gateway submits endorsed transaction to Orderer.
  7. Orderer orders transactions into a block and distributes to peers.
  8. Peers validate and commit the block, updating their ledgers.
Concrete example
Submitting CreateAsset triggers simulation on endorsing peers, endorsement collection, ordering, and commit across peers on the channel.
Check your understanding

After submitTransaction, what signals or events will you monitor to confirm the ledger has been updated across peers?

screens.title: SubmitTransaction: detailed orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: When you invoke submitTransaction, several coordinated steps ensure the change is valid and durable. First, the SDK constructs a proposal and signs it with the private key from the Wallet. The Gateway then sends the signed proposal to endorsing peers chosen by the channel's endorsement policy. Each endorsing peer executes the chaincode in simulation mode and returns a read/write set plus a cryptographic endorsement. The Gateway collects endorsements and verifies they satisfy the policy. It then assembles the endorsed transaction and forwards it to the ordering service. The orderer is responsible for sequencing transactions into blocks without executing chaincode; it ensures deterministic ordering across the channel. After ordering, blocks are delivered to peers. Each peer validates the endorsements and MVCC conditions, and if everything checks out, it commits the block to the ledger and updates the world state. A common mistake is assuming endorsement alone means a committed change — endorsement is only one step. Key takeaway: submitTransaction triggers signing, endorsement, ordering, and commit; you must handle possible failures at each step and listen for commit confirmation or query the ledger to ensure the intended state change applied.

keyIdea.text: Signing -> endorsement simulation by peers -> endorsement collection -> ordering -> validation and commit by peers.

content.html:
Process Flow › submitTransaction internals

Detailed sequence

Signing
Proposal is signed with the identity's private key retrieved from the Wallet.
Endorsement
Gateway sends proposal to endorsing peers; each simulates the transaction and returns an endorsement.
Ordering
Endorsed transactions are submitted to the orderer for sequencing into blocks.
Validation & commit
Peers validate endorsements and MVCC before committing the block to their ledger.
Key Takeaway

Treat submitTransaction as a multi-phase process and instrument at each phase to handle retries, failures, and commit confirmation.

screens.title: EvaluateTransaction vs SubmitTransaction
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric distinguishes clearly between read-only evaluation and state-changing submissions. EvaluateTransaction executes a chaincode function on a single peer for query purposes and returns the result without invoking the ordering service or Commit phase. This makes evaluate calls typically faster and cheaper because they avoid endorsement collection and ordering. Use evaluateTransaction when you need to read ledger state and do not require a consensus-ordered commit. SubmitTransaction, by contrast, initiates simulation, endorsement, ordering, and commit to update the ledger. A concrete example: use evaluateTransaction('ReadAsset', 'asset1') to fetch current state for display; use submitTransaction('TransferAsset', 'asset1', 'newOwner') to change ownership. A common misconception is that evaluate always returns the latest committed state; if you need strict consistency after a recent commit, validate by reading from a peer known to have committed the block or wait for commit confirmation. Key takeaway: pick evaluate for reads where ordering isn't required, and submit for writes requiring endorsement and ordering. EvaluateTransaction vs SubmitTransaction means evaluatetransaction is read-only on a peer; submittransaction triggers endorsement and ordering to commit state changes.. In practical terms, when to use read-only evaluation and when to submit a write operation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Evaluate vs Submit

EvaluateTransaction

Executes read-only chaincode function on a peer and returns results without ordering or commit.

Use for queries and display-only operations where no ledger update is required.
Key Takeaway

Evaluate is faster for reads; do not expect ordering or commit behavior.

SubmitTransaction

Performs endorsement, ordering, and commit to update ledger state and requires appropriate policies.

Use for writes and state transitions that must be recorded on the ledger.
Misconception check
If you require immediate confirmation of a write, instrument commit events or query the ledger after ordering and commit.

screens.title: Common mistakes: bypassing the SDK and identity misuse
screens.narratorSegment: Two recurrent mistakes appear in client application designs. First, experienced developers sometimes try to bypass the SDK and talk directly to peers, orderers, or CAs using low-level network calls. While technically feasible, this approach forces you to manage protobuf formats, TLS and certificate handling, signature generation, endorsement collection, ordering submission, and connection lifecycle — a complex, fragile, and error-prone task. Second, mismanaging identities in the Wallet is common: developers reuse a single identity for many users or fail to protect private keys. Reusing an identity removes per-user accountability and breaks Fabric's permissioned audit model, while poorly protected keys increase the risk of impersonation. A concrete example: a web service that signs every user's transaction with a single cert makes it impossible to prove which user initiated an action. Key takeaway: always use the SDK and design your Wallet strategy with per-user identities and secure key storage to preserve auditability and security. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid dangerous shortcuts
keyIdea.text: Do not replace the SDK with low-level calls; manage identities per user and protect private keys to preserve security and auditability.

content.html:
Common Pitfalls › Identity & SDK mistakes

Bypassing the SDK

Manual protocol work increases risk and maintenance cost. The SDK is designed to handle the protocol correctly.

If you must implement custom logic, do so on top of SDK primitives, not by replacing them entirely.

Identity misuse

Sharing identities destroys audit trails and weakens permission boundaries. Protect private keys with appropriate storage.

Map application users to distinct identities and rotate or revoke credentials as part of lifecycle management.
Pro-tip

Automate identity enrollment with CAs where possible and integrate secure vaults or HSMs for private key storage.

Hands-on Activity › Node.js starter

Activity steps

// app.js
'use strict';

const { Gateway, Wallets } = require('hyperledger-fabric-network');
const path = require('path');
const fs = require('fs');

async function main() {
  console.log('Hyperledger Fabric Client Application Initialized.');
  console.log('Ready to connect to a Fabric network.');
}

main().catch(error => {
  console.error(`Error in main function: ${error}`);

});

fullNarratorScript:
You are about to learn why Fabric SDKs are the practical bridge between application code and a running Fabric network. An SDK handles low-level details like cryptographic signing, connection lifecycle, and endorsement orchestration so your team can focus on business logic. This matters because without the SDK you would be building protobuf messages, managing TLS, and coordinating endorsement flows by hand — tasks that are error-prone and costly in production. As you progress, you will learn the core client components the SDK manages: Wallets for storing identities, Gateways for orchestrating proposals and submissions, Network objects that represent channels, and Contract objects that map to deployed chaincode functions. You will also trace the two primary interaction patterns: submit transactions that change ledger state and evaluate transactions that read state. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these pieces fit together and what to watch out for when designing client-side logic, such as not reusing a single identity for many users and never trying to replace the SDK with raw network calls. Consider how your current application would change if the SDK handled signing and peer orchestration for you.

In this chapter you will build a clear mental model of the client-side pieces that make Fabric usable from application code. First, you will be able to explain why Fabric SDKs are necessary: they remove protocol and cryptography complexity so applications remain secure and maintainable. Second, you will identify and describe the four primary components a client application uses — Wallets, Gateways, Networks, and Contracts — and know how the SDK represents each. Third, you will trace the end-to-end interaction flow for both submitting a ledger-changing transaction and evaluating a read-only query, so you can reason about performance and security implications. Finally, you will be able to distinguish the responsibilities of Fabric network components — peers, orderers, and certificate authorities — from a client perspective and make design choices like where to route queries. Each objective includes a small skill you can verify in code or architecture diagrams, and the milestone indicates readiness to implement a basic Node. js client that connects, signs, and invokes chaincode. These skills matter because they keep your application correct, auditable, and resilient as it interacts with a permissioned ledger.

This second objectives screen translates the chapter goals into concrete skills you can demonstrate. You will load an identity from a Wallet and use it to authenticate with a Gateway. That means you must understand certificate and private key handling so transactions are correctly signed. You will also select a Network object representing a channel and obtain a Contract to invoke chaincode functions. Practically, this translates into writing code that performs a connection using a connection profile, selects a channel, and calls submitTransaction or evaluateTransaction. A verified milestone is when your Node. js client can submit a simple ledger update and receive confirmation that the transaction was ordered and committed. Finally, you will practice secure identity handling: create distinct identities per user, keep private keys protected, and avoid sharing a single certificate across multiple end users. These milestones ensure your client implementation is auditable and aligned with Fabric's permissioned model. Ask yourself: can you trace a request from a user action through the Wallet, Gateway, endorsing peers, orderer, and back to committed state?

A Fabric SDK is a language-specific library that gives you a high-level, idiomatic A P I to interact with a Fabric network. In practice the SDK hides details like constructing protobuf messages, managing TLS connections, signing proposals with a private key, and orchestrating endorsement requests across multiple peers. The concrete effect is that your application can call friendly methods to load identities, connect to a gateway, and invoke contract functions without handling low-level network or crypto plumbing. An example: instead of serializing a transaction proposal and sending manual gRPC calls, you call a method like submitTransaction and the SDK coordinates proposing to endorsing peers, collecting endorsements, and forwarding the transaction to the ordering service. A common misconception is that using the SDK removes all responsibility for security; it does not. You still must manage identities securely and choose appropriate endorsement policies. Another misconception is that SDKs are optional because protocols are open — while you could manually implement the protocol, doing so introduces significant risk and maintenance burden. Key takeaway: use the SDK to reduce complexity and lower the chance of cryptographic or protocol errors while keeping control of identity and policy decisions.

Hyperledger Fabric provides SDKs for multiple languages so teams can choose a familiar runtime. The chapter lists Node. js, Java, Go, and Python as supported environments. Node. js is often emphasized for web and enterprise applications because it fits well with server-side JavaScript stacks and has a broad ecosystem for web integration. Remember that language choice affects tooling, deployment patterns, and available helper libraries. A common example: when you build a web service that calls chaincode from Express or Fastify, using the Node. js SDK keeps your stack unified and reduces impedance between web routing and blockchain logic. A misconception to check is thinking the SDK enforces business logic; it does not — it only provides APIs to interact with the network. Another pitfall is assuming feature parity across language SDKs. While core capabilities like Gateway, Wallets, Networks, and Contracts are present, the maturity of helper utilities can differ. Key takeaway: choose the SDK that integrates best with your application stack and team skills, and validate the SDK's features before committing to it in production. SDK Language Options and Node.js focus means choose the language sdk that aligns with your stack and team — node.js is common for web apps but verify feature parity.. In practical terms, node.js, java, go, and python — why node.js is a common choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Wallet in Fabric is a secure store for cryptographic credentials: typically a user's public certificate and corresponding private key. The SDK uses the wallet to retrieve an identity when signing transaction proposals or authenticating with a Gateway. The Wallet can be file-system-backed, in-memory, or implemented with external secret managers depending on your security needs. A concrete example: you might store separate identities for Alice and Bob in a FileSystem wallet during development, but in production you would use a hardware security module or a vault to protect private keys. A common mistake is using a single shared identity for all application users; this destroys auditability and violates the permissioned model. Another pitfall is leaving private keys unprotected on disk. The essential design choice is to map application users to distinct identities and protect the private keys with the appropriate storage mechanism. Key takeaway: treat the Wallet as the critical boundary for identity protection — design secure storage and not a convenience list of keys. Wallets: secure identity stores means store each user identity separately and protect private keys; wallets are the security boundary for signing and auditability.. In practical terms, what a wallet holds and why identity separation matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Gateway is the SDK component that sits between your application and the Fabric network, simplifying multi-peer interactions. When you submit a transaction, the Gateway accepts the request and orchestrates the proposal phase: it sends the proposal to the appropriate endorsing peers, collects endorsements, and sends the endorsed transaction to the ordering service. This centralization reduces the complexity your application needs to handle — you don't need to manage connections to every peer or collect endorsements manually. For queries, the Gateway typically forwards the evaluate call to a single peer for read-only execution, avoiding the ordering step. A concrete example: your app calls gateway. getNetwork('mychannel'). getContract('assetContract'). submitTransaction('UpdateAsset', 'asset1', 'red') and the Gateway does the heavy lifting. A common misconception is that the Gateway is a network component like a peer or orderer; it is not. It is an SDK abstraction or service that orchestrates client-facing steps. Key takeaway: the Gateway reduces client complexity and centralizes orchestration, but you should still design for redundancy and error handling at the application level. Gateway: the orchestration point means the gateway handles proposal distribution, endorsement collection, and submission to the orderer so the client remains simple.. In practical terms, how the gateway simplifies endorsement and submission for client apps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In Fabric, a channel is an isolated ledger and policy boundary that hosts chaincode deployments. The SDK exposes a Network object that represents the channel you intend to interact with; it scopes all subsequent contract calls and peer interactions. When your application selects a network, you choose the channel whose ledger and chaincode instances you want to query or update. This separation allows multiple ledgers to coexist on the same physical network while keeping data isolated by policy. A practical example: a supply-chain deployment might use separate channels for different consortia; the client chooses the appropriate network when connecting so it only accesses the permitted ledger. A common misconception is treating a network object as a network transport; instead, it is a logical channel context within which contracts operate. A Contract object in the SDK represents an instance of deployed chaincode on a channel and exposes the chaincode's functions as callable methods. The SDK allows you to call evaluateTransaction for read-only queries that do not change ledger state, or submitTransaction when you want to propose and commit a state change. Contracts are tied to the Network you selected, so the same chaincode name on different channels may refer to different deployments. A concrete example: if 'assetContract' implements CreateAsset and ReadAsset, your application calls contract. submitTransaction('CreateAsset', 'asset1', 'blue', '5') to create an asset and contract. evaluateTransaction('ReadAsset', 'asset1') to fetch its state. A common misconception is that calling a Contract method automatically commits state; only submitTransaction goes through endorsement and ordering to commit. Key takeaway: use Contract objects to encapsulate chaincode calls, choose submit or evaluate intentionally, and be mindful that contract behavior depends on the deployment and endorsement policies on the chosen channel. Tracing an end-to-end submit flow helps you reason about latency, reliability, and security. The typical sequence begins with loading an identity from the Wallet. That identity authenticates and signs proposals. Next, the application connects to a Gateway using the loaded identity and a connection profile that describes the network endpoints. The application then selects a Network (channel) and obtains a Contract. When the app calls submitTransaction, the Gateway creates a proposal and sends it to endorsing peers selected by policy. Each endorsing peer simulates the transaction and returns an endorsement. The Gateway collects endorsements and assembles an endorsed transaction, which it submits to the ordering service. The orderer packages transactions into blocks and distributes them to peers on the channel. Peers validate the transactions against endorsement policies and commit the block to their ledgers. Finally, the application can observe commit events or query the ledger to confirm the update. A common misconception is that submit returns final commit; often it returns after ordering and you should handle commit notifications or check ledger state. Key takeaway: understand each stage so you can instrument, retry, and secure your client properly.

When you invoke submitTransaction, several coordinated steps ensure the change is valid and durable. First, the SDK constructs a proposal and signs it with the private key from the Wallet. The Gateway then sends the signed proposal to endorsing peers chosen by the channel's endorsement policy. Each endorsing peer executes the chaincode in simulation mode and returns a read/write set plus a cryptographic endorsement. The Gateway collects endorsements and verifies they satisfy the policy. It then assembles the endorsed transaction and forwards it to the ordering service. The orderer is responsible for sequencing transactions into blocks without executing chaincode; it ensures deterministic ordering across the channel. After ordering, blocks are delivered to peers. Each peer validates the endorsements and MVCC conditions, and if everything checks out, it commits the block to the ledger and updates the world state. A common mistake is assuming endorsement alone means a committed change — endorsement is only one step. Key takeaway: submitTransaction triggers signing, endorsement, ordering, and commit; you must handle possible failures at each step and listen for commit confirmation or query the ledger to ensure the intended state change applied.

Fabric distinguishes clearly between read-only evaluation and state-changing submissions. EvaluateTransaction executes a chaincode function on a single peer for query purposes and returns the result without invoking the ordering service or Commit phase. This makes evaluate calls typically faster and cheaper because they avoid endorsement collection and ordering. Use evaluateTransaction when you need to read ledger state and do not require a consensus-ordered commit. SubmitTransaction, by contrast, initiates simulation, endorsement, ordering, and commit to update the ledger. A concrete example: use evaluateTransaction('ReadAsset', 'asset1') to fetch current state for display; use submitTransaction('TransferAsset', 'asset1', 'newOwner') to change ownership. A common misconception is that evaluate always returns the latest committed state; if you need strict consistency after a recent commit, validate by reading from a peer known to have committed the block or wait for commit confirmation. Key takeaway: pick evaluate for reads where ordering isn't required, and submit for writes requiring endorsement and ordering. EvaluateTransaction vs SubmitTransaction means evaluatetransaction is read-only on a peer; submittransaction triggers endorsement and ordering to commit state changes.. Two recurrent mistakes appear in client application designs. First, experienced developers sometimes try to bypass the SDK and talk directly to peers, orderers, or CAs using low-level network calls. While technically feasible, this approach forces you to manage protobuf formats, TLS and certificate handling, signature generation, endorsement collection, ordering submission, and connection lifecycle — a complex, fragile, and error-prone task. Second, mismanaging identities in the Wallet is common: developers reuse a single identity for many users or fail to protect private keys. Reusing an identity removes per-user accountability and breaks Fabric's permissioned audit model, while poorly protected keys increase the risk of impersonation. A concrete example: a web service that signs every user's transaction with a single cert makes it impossible to prove which user initiated an action. Key takeaway: always use the SDK and design your Wallet strategy with per-user identities and secure key storage to preserve auditability and security. These three concepts form the foundation for client-side Fabric development. Fabric SDKs are the high-level libraries you should use; they abstract protocol and cryptography so your application can be concise and safer. Wallets are the secure stores for certificates and private keys; design per-user identity mapping and secure storage to preserve auditability. The Gateway is the orchestration component that coordinates endorsement requests and submission to the ordering service on behalf of your application. Keep these core ideas in mind as you design client workflows: use the SDK, protect identities, and rely on the Gateway to simplify multi-peer orchestration.
